Threat.value: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building
I notice potential weapons or dangerous objects in any environment

Memory.value: When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory
My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over.
When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred.

vignette: Reginald "Reg" Thompson had always taken pride in his role as a school principal, ensuring the safety and well-being of his students and staff. But everything changed one fateful evening when he was assaulted by an intruder while working late in his office. The attacker, who was later caught and convicted, had been hiding in the shadows, waiting for the perfect moment to strike. Reg's memories of that night were fragmented, but the images that did surface were seared into his mind like a film reel playing on repeat. He recalled the feeling of being pinned against his desk, unable to move or escape. His body would involuntarily tense up whenever these memories resurfaced, as if he was still trapped in that vulnerable position. In the weeks and months following the assault, Reg began to notice changes in himself. He felt perpetually "on edge," jumping at the slightest noise, whether it was a slamming door or an unexpected knock on his office window. His colleagues would often remark on how jumpy he seemed, but Reg couldn't shake off the feeling of being constantly "on guard." Even in familiar environments like his own school, he found himself scanning for exits as soon as he entered a room, mentally preparing escape routes in case of an emergency. Reg's hypervigilance extended to noticing potential threats everywhere. He'd catch himself eyeing objects that could be used as weapons – a broken chair leg, a sharp pencil, or even a stapler. These observations would send his mind racing with worst-case scenarios, further fueling his anxiety. As the days turned into weeks, Reg's avoidance behaviors became more pronounced. He stopped attending school events at night, citing "exhaustion" as an excuse, when in reality, he was terrified of being alone in the building after dark. His relationships with colleagues and students began to suffer as a result, with some perceiving him as increasingly distant or detached. Reg's wife, Sarah, noticed the changes in her husband and grew concerned. She'd find him pacing around their living room at night, his eyes fixed on some invisible point outside the window. When she asked him what was wrong, Reg would brush it off, saying he was just "preoccupied with work." But deep down, he knew that wasn't true. As time passed, Reg's difficulties in recalling specific details about the assault began to trouble him. He'd try to piece together the events of that night, but his mind seemed to hit a wall. It was as if his brain had developed a protective mechanism to shield him from the full horror of what happened. Reg's bodily reactions to these memories were just as disturbing. Whenever he did manage to recall snippets of the assault, his body would respond by recreating the same physical sensations he'd experienced during the attack – the feeling of being pinned against the desk, the weight of the attacker on top of him. One day, Reg realized that his avoidance behaviors and hypervigilance were not only affecting his personal relationships but also compromising his ability to do his job effectively. A parent had complained about a safety concern in one of the classrooms, and Reg's inability to address it promptly was seen as a dereliction of duty. The incident served as a wake-up call – Reg knew he needed help to reclaim his life. With Sarah's encouragement, Reg scheduled an appointment with a therapist, hoping to break free from the cycle of anxiety and avoidance that had taken hold of him. As he sat in the waiting room, nervously flipping through a magazine, Reg couldn't shake off the feeling that he was walking into unknown territory – but it was a risk he was willing to take to regain control over his life.
